claim: go-hass-agent is a dual-transport agent: it registers with Home Assistant as a mobile_app device via the Native App Integration API (long-lived token) and cannot run in MQTT-only mode, while an optional MQTT v5 side adds controls and additional sensors
stance_target: an MQTT-only architecture (ha-linux-agent's rumqttc path) diverges from the most mature Linux agent; the native HA API is a hard dependency for go-hass-agent's identity model
scope_conditions: go-hass-agent current main (v14.x era); requires MQTT v5 broker for the MQTT side
quoted_support: Unfortunately no, Go Hass Agent cannot run in an MQTT-only credentials. It makes use of the Native App Integration API that is not MQTT only. ... Go Hass Agent requires MQTT v5 support on your MQTT broker.

claim: go-hass-agent's Linux sensor surface is sourced from D-Bus (logind sessions, power state, screen lock, NetworkManager connections/Wi-Fi, XDG portal active-app/desktop settings, UPower battery, MPRIS, fwupd), ProcFS (memory, disk usage, load, CPU usage/frequency, uptime, kernel, distro, CPU vulns), SysFS (disk IO rates, hwmon hardware sensors), Netlink (link states/rates), and geoclue (location), each with its own update cadence from ~5s (disk/network rates) to ~15min (uptime, ABRT)
stance_target: the ha-linux-agent redesign should mirror this layered source map — it is the de-facto Linux companion sensor contract, and it shows which subsystems are event-driven (D-Bus) vs polled (ProcFS/SysFS)
scope_conditions: Linux only; sensors degrade individually when the required daemon (logind, NetworkManager, PipeWire, fwupd, geoclue, systemd-oomd, ABRT) is absent
quoted_support: Active App and Total Running Apps ... Via D-Bus (requires XDG Desktop Portal Support support). ... Memory Stats ... Sourced via ProcFS. Updated ~every minute. ... Both sourced via SysFS. Updated ~every 5 seconds. ... Device/Link State Via Netlink.

claim: Disk SMART monitoring in go-hass-agent requires file capabilities on the binary (cap_sys_rawio, cap_sys_admin, cap_mknod, cap_dac_override=+ep) which the rpm/deb/arch packages and containers apply automatically, and user-activity detection requires cap_setgid/cap_setuid plus membership of the input group
stance_target: privilege on a Linux HA agent is per-capability, not per-root; a NixOS fleet agent needs a wrapper or service-hardening story that grants exactly these capability sets
scope_conditions: Linux; capabilities applied by packaging or setcap manually when self-built
quoted_support: Requires the following capabilities on the Go Hass Agent binary (already applied for containers and rpm/deb/arch packages): cap_sys_rawio,cap_sys_admin,cap_mknod,cap_dac_override=+ep. ... Requires user running Go Hass Agent is in the input group.

claim: go-hass-agent refuses to run as root and must run as a regular user; privilege elevation for scripts is delegated to the scripts themselves
stance_target: running a fleet-wide agent as a root/system service (as a NixOS system-level daemon on every host would naturally do); the mature precedent insists on a user-level daemon with enable-linger
quoted_support: You cannot run Go Hass Agent with root privileges or as the root user. The agent will refuse to run. ... You will also need to ensure your user has "lingering" enabled. Run loginctl list-users and check that your user has LINGER set to "yes".

claim: go-hass-agent supports containerised deployment with alternative system mount points via PROCFS_ROOT, DEVFS_ROOT, SYSFS_ROOT environment variables, with host /proc, /sys, /run/dbus and the user session bus mounted read-only, plus SYS_ADMIN/SYS_RAWIO/MKNOD capabilities added
stance_target: the jupiterOS fleet agent needs a container-friendly sensor path (or equivalent NixOS sandbox escape hatches) for hosts where the agent runs in a container or confined service
scope_conditions: podman/docker; Alpine-based ghcr.io multiarch images (amd64, armv6/v7, arm64)
quoted_support: PROCFS_ROOT: alternative mount point for /proc. DEVFS_ROOT: alternative mount point for /dev. SYSFS_ROOT: alternative mount point for /sys. When these are set, any sensors that would normally source their data from a file in one of the canonical system mount points, will use the alternative mount point location specified.

claim: go-hass-agent's MQTT controls include arbitrary D-Bus method invocation via JSON payloads on the topic gohassagent/HOSTNAME/dbuscommand, plus a commands.toml file defining button, switch, and number controls that run executables without a shell and WITHOUT state synchronisation back to HA
stance_target: both the power (arbitrary D-Bus control surface) and the pitfall (no state round-trip for custom controls) that ha-linux-agent's command design must weigh; MQTT v5 required
scope_conditions: MQTT configured; commands run as the agent user; no glob/pipeline/redirection
quoted_support: The agent will subscribe to the MQTT topic gohassagent/HOSTNAME/dbuscommand ... States are not kept in sync. This is most important for all controls besides buttons. For example, if you configure a switch, any changes to the state you make outside of Home Assistant will not be reflected in Home Assistant automatically.

claim: go-hass-agent script sensors accept any shebang script (bash, python, etc.) emitting JSON/YAML/TOML with a schedule field using Quartz cron expressions or @every <duration> intervals, and each script can emit multiple sensors with icon, state, units, device_class, state_class, and attributes
stance_target: a declarative script-sensor extension mechanism (cron-scheduled, multi-format, self-describing) is the proven extensibility pattern ha-linux-agent is probably missing
scope_conditions: scripts in the config dir scripts/ folder, executable by the agent user, run without user interaction; agent does no sanitisation of output
quoted_support: Each script run by the agent can create one or more sensors and each script can run on its own schedule, specified using a Cron syntax. ... Go Hass Agent makes no attempt to do any analysis or sanitization of script output, other than ensuring the output is a supported format.

claim: When both transports are enabled the device appears TWICE in Home Assistant — once under the Mobile App integration (sensors) and once under the MQTT integration (controls) — and HA's architecture does not allow them to be combined
stance_target: ha-linux-agent's MQTT-only design avoids this split-brain device identity problem that even the mature dual-transport agent cannot solve
scope_conditions: go-hass-agent with MQTT enabled; Home Assistant architecture limitation
quoted_support: Go Hass Agent will appear in two places in your Home Assistant. Firstly, under the Mobile App integration, which will show all the sensors ... Secondly, under the MQTT integration ... Unfortunately, due to limitations with the Home Assistant architecture, these cannot be combined in a single place.

claim: go-hass-agent reports resource usage of well under 50 MB of memory with very little CPU, uses D-Bus signals for event-driven sensors, and applies jitter to polling intervals to avoid a thundering-herd problem
stance_target: fleet-wide deployment on every jupiterOS host is resource-feasible; a Linux agent should be event-driven over D-Bus and jitter its polls — design guidance for ha-linux-agent
quoted_support: On Linux, the agent with all sensors working, should consume well less than 50 MB of memory with very little CPU usage. ... For sensors that are polled on an interval, the agent makes use of some jitter in the polling intervals to avoid a "thundering herd" problem.

claim: go-hass-agent disables a sensor group via the preferences file and can also react to HA-side entity disabling; however HA-side disabling does NOT stop raw data gathering, only preferences-side disabling does
stance_target: the agent-vs-HA sensor-control boundary matters for fleet resource tuning on low-power hosts
quoted_support: Note that disabling a sensor in Home Assistant will not stop Go Hass Agent from gathering the raw data for the sensor. Only disabling it via the Agent preferences file will stop any data gathering.

claim: go-hass-agent's hardware sensors report raw hwmon values without chip-dependent scaling, so they can disagree with lm-sensors output; transformation is deferred to HA template sensors
stance_target: any assumption that hardware sensor values from a Linux agent are display-ready; a fleet agent that wants turnkey hwmon parity must implement lm-sensors-style chip scaling itself
quoted_support: Go Hass Agent sends the raw hardware sensor data without any chip-dependent scaling/transformation. If you are comparing the values to, say, the output of sensors from the sensors command (part of lm-sensors), there will be discrepancies; lm-sensors has a database of chips with scaling/transformation information ... Future versions of Go Hass Agent will hopefully use similar logic.

claim: Sensors or controls on one host are gated by significant privilege discrepancy: HA offers no fine-grained access control for exposed controls, so ANY Home Assistant user can trigger ANY control on ANY device running an agent
stance_target: fleet-wide command execution is a security surface ha-linux-agent must treat seriously (per-host command allowlists, MQTT topic ACLs, or broker-level authz)
scope_conditions: go-hass-agent custom controls; applies equally to any companion agent exposing commands
quoted_support: Home Assistant does not currently offer any fine-grained access control for controls like the above. So any Home Assistant user will be able to run any of the controls. This means that a Home Assistant user not associated with the device user running the agent can use the exposed controls to issue potentially disruptive actions on a device that another user is accessing.
